pos.personaBrief: Gap axis (no verified possession evidence): from general knowledge, Cullis's Wolves were a fast, direct side that used pace and wingers to exploit space rather than a possession team, which fits the 'kick and rush' label and the verified quick distribution to Mullen and Hancocks (gameofthepeople, 2019). Ball retention is not what the profile valued.

pro.personaBrief: Verified: the side played 'kick and rush' in the rivals' label, with 'quick distribution from the defence out to Mullen and Hancocks' (gameofthepeople, 2019) and a sophisticated direct style that relied on pace and aggression (TFT). The forward pass and the early long ball to pace are the core of this progression, while the patient build-up is not evidenced.

est.personaBrief: Verified: a rigid, system-driven side with a set forward line (Hancocks, Wilshaw, Swinbourne) and wide wingers (TFT 1953-54), run by a manager who imposed discipline (Cullis's strict-discipline ethos, unverified). Fixed positions and touchline wingers fit this, while the rondo-style close combination and the drop-off striker are not what the sources describe.

lar.personaBrief: Verified: 'Wingers were very important to the way Cullis's team played' and the 1953-54 side's speed came from Hancocks and Mullen (TFT, 2016); the 1957-60 crosses from wide players confirm the flank route (gameofthepeople, 2019). The width-by-the-flanks profile is the strongest-evidenced axis in the file.

blo.personaBrief: Gap axis (no verified defensive-block evidence): from general knowledge, the Wolves of this era defended with half-backs in a compact, fairly deep shape and did not press high as a system, which is consistent with the verified 'fitness, pace and aggression' description and with the counter-attacking reliance on wingers.

mar.personaBrief: Gap axis (marking not verified in any source read): from general knowledge, British defences of the 1950s, and Wolves' centre-halves, marked man-to-man, with the centre-half taking the opposing centre-forward. This matches the strong, individual defensive identity implied by the half-back line named in the sources.

pla.personaBrief: Verified: the 1953-54 and 1958-59 teams kept 'the same side and the same style of play' across the decade (TFT, 2016), and Cullis's sacking and tenure was built on a fixed identity. The profile trusts its style, changes little, and imposes it, but does not reshape itself to each opponent.

res.personaBrief: Verified: the trophies (First Division 1953-54, 1957-58, 1958-59; FA Cup 1949 and 1960; Charity Shields) show that winning mattered, while the 'kick and rush' label was critics' language and the team's style was defended as its own (Wikipedia honours list; TFT). Results and style both counted, so the purpose is mixed, and the first question is genuinely indifferent to this profile.

sis.personaBrief: Verified: 'Cullis placed huge emphasis on fitness and power' and the system was the basis of the team (TFT, undated), and the manager's approach was built around collective discipline. The side valued a drilled structure and everyone doing the job over individual freedom, though the sources also credit wingers' pace.

jog.personaBrief: Gap axis (no verified player-type evidence beyond the undated 'fitness and power' remark): from general knowledge, the Wolves of Cullis valued strength, stamina and pace, and the classic creative number 10 was not the profile's priority, which is consistent with the physical, aggressive description.

bas.personaBrief: Verified: the FA Youth Cup was won in 1958 and runner-up in 1953, 1954 and 1962 (Wikipedia honours list), showing a functioning youth system. Squad selection from youth is not verified, but the profile developed kids while still winning with seasoned players.

lid.personaBrief: Gap axis (no verified leadership evidence): from general knowledge, Cullis was a strict, authoritarian disciplinarian who inherited Buckley's 'strict discipline, giving your all in training' ethos (gameofthepeople, 2019, undated) and was sacked for his control rather than for his harmony, so the coach was the boss and the rules applied equally.
